1:
The psalm stands as the companion and answer to the twentieth, and the witnesses open by hearing in it the thanksgiving that crowns the earlier prayer. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the two side by side: where the people had cried “Jahve fulfil all thy desires” as they interceded for their king, here they can thankfully say “the desire of his heart hast Thou granted,” the one psalm bringing wishes and prayers, the other thanksgivings and hopes after the king’s recovery and in the certainty of a victorious war. They note that the Targum and the Talmud understand the psalm of the king Messiah, and that Rashi would give up that reading “for the sake of the Christians”; yet, they add, the pair treats of David, whose cause, moving through suffering toward triumph, is figuratively the cause of Christ. The reformed John Calvin reads it as a public and solemn thanksgiving for the king’s prosperity, its subject almost one with the preceding, and finds the Spirit’s design above all to direct the minds of the faithful to Christ, “the end and perfection of this kingdom,” under whom alone they could be saved.

Over the opening line, “the king shall joy in thy strength, O LORD,” the schools converge on the source of the joy. Calvin paraphrases, “Lord, in putting forth thy power to sustain the king, thou wilt preserve him,” so that, ascribing his safety to God’s power, he greatly rejoices in Him. The reformed John Gill weighs whether the strength be that everlasting strength which is in Jehovah himself and the same in Christ as the mighty God, or the strength communicated to Christ as man to complete the work of redemption. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears David professing that his joy was in God’s strength and salvation, not in the strength or success of his armies, and directing his subjects to the same, all with an eye to Christ, of whose triumphs over darkness David’s victories were but shadows. His fellow Charles Spurgeon lifts the whole to the throne: Jesus is the King, proclaimed such even on the cross, who as man found his strength in Jehovah and now, “anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows,” joys in the power of the Lord.

The latin-fathers Augustine reads the title and line directly of Christ: in Thy strength “whereby the Word was made flesh, the Man Christ Jesus shall rejoice.” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, surveying the occasion, weighs whether the song celebrates the victory over Sennacherib, or Hezekiah’s added years, or, most likely, David’s conquest of Rabbah, whose king’s crown David set on his own head, before owning that many refer the whole to the Messiah — the Targum’s “melech Meshicha,” the King Messiah. Ellicott renders the line “the king is exulting in thy might,” the victory he prayed for now secured.
2:
The thanksgiving names its ground, that every petition of the king has been granted — “thou hast given him his heart’s desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips.” The reformed John Gill hears the very prayer of the preceding psalm answered, where the church had asked the Lord to grant the king his heart’s desire and fulfil all his counsel (Ps. 20:4); whatever Christ’s heart desired or his lips requested, Gill says, has been given him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the line the same way, as referring back to the prayers offered in that twentieth psalm, the request and its answer standing to each other as the two panels of a single picture.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the wording and the occasion it half discloses. He notes that the Hebrew word rendered “request” occurs nowhere else in Scripture and is connected with a root meaning to be poor and therefore in want, and that the negative is emphatic — “the request of his lips thou hast by no means withheld.” From the prayer for length of life named in v.4 he draws the suggestion that this request was uttered in sickness, while owning that the general tone of the psalm, with its note of triumph, connects it rather with a victory; and he leaves the reader to feel the double possibility without forcing the choice. It is a fine instance of the school’s caution, that a single rare word will not bear the whole weight of a reconstructed occasion.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, keep the verse within the movement of the paired psalms: the people who in the former poem came before God with their wishes and prayers for their king now come with their thanksgivings, so that the granted desire of this line is the answering echo of the petition they had lately raised. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Whether the king’s request rose from a sick-bed or from the field of a finished war, they agree that the verse celebrates a prayer heard and a desire met, and that the God who withholds nothing good from his anointed has here given him the very thing his heart and lips had asked — the surest ground, Gill adds, on which a delivered people may build their song.
3:
The reason of the joy is now traced to a grace that runs ahead of the asking, for God “preventest him with the blessings of goodness.” The witnesses linger, as they must, over the old word “prevent.” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes it from the Latin praevenio, to go before, recalling the collect of the Liturgy, “Prevent us, O Lord, in all our doings,” and rendering the Hebrew tekademennu “thou shalt go before him with the blessings of goodness”; he even reaches for Henry V’s word before Agincourt, “God before,” to catch the sense of a mercy that leads the way. His fellow John Wesley reads the same note plainly: God crowns him “with manifold blessings, both more and sooner than he expected.” The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses it “comest to meet him,” the same familiar sense of the collect.

The reformed John Gill hears the word disclose three things at once about the blessings of a spiritual, not a temporal, goodness: the freeness of the gift, given before it could well be asked; its earliness, laid up in Christ before his incarnation, from the very foundation of the world; and its order, coming first to Christ and then to his people in him. To be prevented with grace is, for Gill, to be met by a goodness that neither waits for merit nor lingers upon prayer.

Over the second line, “thou settest a crown of pure gold upon his head,” the witnesses part company. Clarke takes it for a plain fact of history, the crown of the king of Rabbah, which David lifted from the conquered city and set upon his own head (2 Sam. 12:30). Ellicott is less sure: some, he grants, identify it with that crown of Rabbah, others make it the token of a coronation, and Ewald thought of a birthday celebration; but probably no more is meant than a symbol of victory and rejoicing, such as the maidens offered a monarch returning in triumph, a garland of gladness rather than a diadem of gold. So the schools divide over the crown — whether it be the literal spoil of a stormed capital or the emblematic wreath of a festal welcome — though not over the mercy that sets it there, a goodness that goes before the king and rests, unbidden, upon his head.
4:
Now the thanksgiving reaches the line the witnesses find most charged, the grant of life that runs out to “length of days for ever and ever.” The reformed John Gill takes the asked-for life two ways at once: Christ as man, about to die, asked and received resurrection life, and asked life too for his people, that they might live spiritually and eternally, so that life is given to him for them, and he has power to bestow it on as many as the Father has given him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep to the movement of the strophe, reading how the help of God turns to the king’s honour and enables him to maintain and strengthen his kingship with fame and glory, the divine investiture that the next verse will name.

But the words “for ever and ever” open a genuine division. The wesleyan-arminian voices press them toward Christ. Clarke notes that the verse has driven some to read the whole psalm of Hezekiah’s sickness and his added fifteen years, but takes it more literally of the Messiah, of whom David was the type and representative. Wesley allows the first sense — God gave David a long life and reign, then translated him to live for ever — but finds it “more eminently fulfilled in Christ,” who asked to be saved from death (Heb. 5:7) and, his temporal life taken, instantly received another far nobler, an everlasting life in soul and body at the Father’s right hand. Gill too hears the eternal life of the Redeemer and his people.

Against this the other grammatical-historical witness sets a sober caution. Charles Ellicott holds that “for ever and ever” is merely a term for indefinite length, the very phrase of the courtly salutation with which a king was hailed (1 Kings 1:31), and warns that “an allusion to the eternal kingdom of the Messiah is not to be forced on the passage.” So the debate is real and unresolved: whether the length of days reaches, with Clarke and Wesley and Gill, to the deathless reign of Christ, or names, with Ellicott, no more than the full and honoured life a grateful people wished their king. The witnesses divide not over the grant of life but over how far its “for ever” is meant to stretch.
5:
“His glory is great in thy salvation” — and the witnesses trace the greatness at once to its source. The reformed John Gill refers the glory to the King Messiah, made great in the Lord’s salvation of him: delivered from all his sorrows, raised from the dead, set at God’s right hand and crowned with honour; or else made great in the salvation of his people wrought by him, so that the glory of the deliverance rebounds upon the Deliverer. The point, for Gill, is that the king’s renown is not self-derived but is the reflected splendour of what God has done for him and through him.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the same lesson. Adam Clarke grants the glory to be great, but insists that “it had its greatness from God’s salvation,” for there is no true nobility but of the soul, and the soul has none save what it receives from the grace and salvation of God. John Wesley reads “glory” as the king’s fame and renown, and refers it to the great and glorious deliverances God had wrought “both for him and by him” — the double preposition catching how the victory was at once granted to the king and achieved through him.

Upon the second clause, “honour and majesty hast thou laid upon him,” the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology. The verb, they observe, is the word used of divine investiture and endowment (Ps. 89:20), so that the honour and majesty are not the king’s own attainment but a robe laid upon him by the hand of God, who clothes his anointed as he pleases. The witnesses do not divide: they read the verse as one confession that whatever weight of glory rests on the king is a burden God has laid, a majesty conferred and not seized, so that the salvation which delivers him is the very fountain of the honour that crowns him, and the praise of it returns, by every voice here, to the God who wrought it.
6:
The ground of the king’s gladness is now carried to its height, for God has “made him most blessed for ever.” The witnesses fasten on the Hebrew idiom beneath the phrase. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the words are literally “blessings,” a plural of fulness like the opening of the Psalter’s first psalm, so that the king is not merely blessed but made a very sum and treasury of blessing. The reformed John Gill reads the same idiom, “thou hast set him to be blessings for ever,” and unfolds it of the Mediator: not as God, who is over all blessed and needs no making so, but as man, appointed to be blessings to his people — redemption to free them, righteousness to justify, sanctification, wisdom, and strength — all of them irreversible, never repented of nor taken away.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the literal “Thou hast set him for blessings for ever,” and makes the Messiah the very source whence all blessings for time and eternity are drawn; and on the second clause he hears the note of the finished work — Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him,” endured the cross and is now set down at God’s right hand, exceeding glad. His fellow John Wesley glosses that gladness simply, God “smiling upon him by his grace and favour.” Ellicott sharpens the closing phrase, preferring “in thy presence” to “with thy countenance” (Ps. 16:11), the joy being the fulness of an intimate fellowship with God.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the verse as a hinge, for here the second half of the psalm commences and the address, hitherto directed to God, begins to turn toward the king himself, no longer in the accent of wish but of confident expectation. The witnesses do not divide: they read the line as the summit of the thanksgiving, the king made a fountain of everlasting blessing and filled with the gladness of God’s own presence, before the poem wheels about to face the enemies over whom that blessedness will presently be shown to triumph.
7:
With the seventh verse the psalm passes from thanksgiving to a settled confidence, resting the whole on the king’s trust — “for the king trusteth in the LORD.” The reformed John Gill takes the king for the Messiah, after the Targum, and reads a trust reaching through his sufferings as man: he trusted the Lord for support and sustenance, for help in trouble and deliverance out of it, that he would be heard both for himself and for his people, and be glorified with all honour and blessedness. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it the disclaimer of a true conqueror: “it was not by my skill or valour that I gained this victory, but by faith in the strong protecting arm of Jehovah”; and the “shall not be moved” he refers best to David’s great prototype, whose throne and kingdom and government shall remain for ever.

The puritan-evangelical voices dwell on the security of that trust. Matthew Henry, opening here the long meditation that carries to the psalm’s end, makes the joy and confidence of the king the ground of all his people’s: as the king rejoices in God (v.1), so his subjects will be thankful; as the king trusts in God, so they will be encouraged. Through the mercy of the Most High, and not through any merit or strength of his own, he shall not be moved — his prosperous state undisturbed, his faith and hope unshaken — for the mercy of God is enough to secure our happiness, and our trust in that mercy enough to silence all our fears.

Charles Spurgeon presses the same confidence to its Christian height. Our Lord, like a true King, was a master of the shield of faith, safe in his Father’s care until his hour was come, committing his cause to Him that judges right and his spirit at last into the same hands; the joy of the earlier verses was the joy of faith, and “a holy confidence in Jehovah is the true mother of victories.” Eternal mercy, Spurgeon adds, secures the mediatorial throne: other empires dissolve with the lapse of years, but the King in Zion reigns on, the same yesterday, today, and for ever. The witnesses do not divide: the king’s immovable standing rests not on his own arm but on the mercy of the Most High in whom he trusts.
8:
At this verse the poem visibly turns, and the witnesses mark the shift of address before they weigh its threat. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the psalm has hitherto been spoken to Jehovah, but now, “in prophetic strain,” it turns to the king, so that the “thine hand” which “shall find out all thine enemies” is the king’s own. His fellow Keil and Delitzsch read the same, ascribing the destructive effect not to God’s face but to the personal appearing of the king (2 Sam. 17:11), and recalling how David’s arrival before Rabbath Ammon decided its fall, some of its people perishing under instruments of torture and others cast into the brick-kilns (2 Sam. 12:26).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the stress on the reach of the searching hand: “thy uncontrollable power shall find out all thine enemies, wheresoever hidden or howsoever secret,” for God knows the secret sinner and where the workers of iniquity hide themselves. The finding out is not a hunt through the dark but the certain reach of an omniscient power from which no concealment avails.

The reformed John Gill widens the enemies into a long prophetic muster, reading the king as Christ: the Jews who would not have him reign and who crucified him and persecuted his apostles; the Gentiles concerned in his death; the persecuting emperors of Rome; the followers of the man of sin who oppose Christ in his offices and grace; the merely nominal professors who are his enemies in doctrine or in practice; and behind them all the devil and his angels. These, Gill says, the hand of Christ will surely find out, for being omniscient he knows where every foe is and being omnipotent he will lay hold and none shall escape. The witnesses do not divide over the certainty of the reckoning; they agree that the same hand which had crowned and blessed the king is now stretched out to search his enemies to their last hiding-place, whether one reads them as the flesh-and-blood foes of David before Rabbah or as the whole succession of those who set themselves against the Anointed.
9:
“Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger” — and the image, arresting as it is, sets the witnesses to work on both its wording and its source. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses that, as it stands, the figure is obscure, since here it is the fire and not the blackness of the oven that must be the point; a very slight literal change, he argues, gives the sense plainly required, “Thou shalt put them into a fiery oven,” the picture drawn not from Sodom but from a smelter’s furnace (Mal. 3:3), and he reads “the time of thine anger” as literally “of thy face,” the dread majesty by whose very appearing the wicked wither — a power here ascribed to the king, though the poet, startled by the boldness of his own figure, at once refers it back to Jehovah “in his wrath,” literally “in his nostril.”

The reformed John Gill weighs the same alternatives. Some, he notes, find in the oven an allusion to David’s causing the Ammonites to pass through the brick-kiln, others to the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah; and he too allows the rendering “thou shalt put them into a fiery oven,” “as” standing for “into.” Wicked men, he says, are as dry trees and stubble, fit fuel for the furnace of God’s wrath, which is poured forth as fire — a doom he sees begun at Jerusalem’s destruction and to be filled up when Babylon is burned.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the received figure and read its force. Adam Clarke hears that “by thy wrath they shall be burnt up,” and adds a grim turn, that one class of sinners shall be made the means of consuming another. John Wesley glosses the oven in a line: they shall be “like wood, which, when it is cast in, is quickly consumed.” So a real difference runs beneath the verse — whether the enemies are made to resemble a fiery oven, as the text reads, or are cast into one, as Ellicott and Gill would mend it, and whether the fire be borrowed from the overthrow of Sodom, the brick-kilns of Rabbah, or the smelter’s crucible. The witnesses do not divide over the substance, the sudden and utter consuming of the king’s foes; they differ only over the exact shape and provenance of the flame.
10:
The judgment now reaches beyond the men themselves to all that would outlast them, for “their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.” The reformed John Gill reads the “fruit” of the offspring of wicked men, the fruit of the womb, one with the “seed” of the parallel clause, so that the sentence falls not on a generation only but on its succession. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense from the Hebrew, glossing “their fruit” more fully as the “fruit of the womb” (Ps. 127:3), the children in whom a man hopes to survive himself.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses draw out the completeness of the ruin. Adam Clarke: “even their posterity shall be cut off, and thus their memorial shall perish,” the very name of the wicked blotted from remembrance. John Wesley makes the figure sharper still — God “will take away both root and branch, the parents and all that wicked race” — so that the sentence is not the felling of a single tree but the grubbing up of the whole stock.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, sets the verse within the closing strophe as the merited frustration of the enemies’ own design: the fate that overtakes their seed is the just recoil of the evil they had inclined against the king, an evil now made to fall back and bury their line. The witnesses do not divide. They read the destroying of fruit and seed neither as a stray cruelty nor as vengeance on the innocent, but as the extinction of a persistent enmity that would, if left to breed, hand down its quarrel with the Anointed from father to son; and they agree that where the wickedness is rooted out, its memorial and its offspring perish together, leaving no heir to take up the unfinished feud against the throne God has established.
11:
The ground of so heavy a sentence is now laid bare, that the enemies “intended evil against thee” and “imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform.” The reformed John Gill reads the charge to its root: all evil, whether of thought or of deed, is ultimately against the Lord, whose law it transgresses and whose honour it slights; every sin is a hostility committed against God, or against his Anointed, or against his people, who are one with him. The very intention of evil is itself evil, Gill insists, cognizable by the God who reads the heart and punishable by him though it never ripen into act.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the impotence of the plot. Adam Clarke marks the mercy hidden in the limit: “sinners shall not be permitted to do all that is in their power against the godly, much less shall they be able to perform all that they wish.” John Wesley fixes the object of the malice: the evil was intended “against God, not directly, but by consequence,” because it was aimed at David whom God had anointed, and at the Lord’s people, whose injuries God takes as done to himself. The blow struck at the king lands, in God’s reckoning, upon God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the syntax into a concession, rendering the verse, “though they have intended evil against thee, have plotted mischief, they have no power at all.” The clause the Authorized Version turns as a bare statement he reads as a triumphant contrast: the design was real, the malice deep, the device cunningly imagined, and yet the whole came to nothing, for the plotters were left without strength to execute it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the enmity was genuine and God-ward, reaching past the king to the God whose cause he bore, and that its very failure is the point — a mischief conceived with the whole heart and yet still-born, because the arm that would have carried it was never suffered to strike.
12:
The frustrated plot issues in flight, for God will “make them turn their back” when he makes ready his arrows against their faces. The reformed John Gill offers the range of the phrase: the enemies are made to flee and hide from the wrath of God, though to no purpose; or the words may be read “make them turn behind thy back,” God turning his back upon them and regarding them no more; or, with the Targum’s “shoulder,” they are set apart together for destruction, as the goats are severed from the sheep. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the idiom literally — “for thou shalt put them shoulder,” the Vulgate’s pones eos dorsum — and, weighing Ewald’s “shalt strike them back,” judges that the received version explains it rightly, comparing the like expression of giving an enemy’s neck (Ps. 18:40).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns from the grammar to the scene of rout. God, he says, can in a moment strike the most powerful and numerous army with panic, even in the very moment of victory, so that even the lame take the prey and divide the spoil; and to aim “against the face of them” is to make them turn their backs and fly “as if a volley of arrows had been discharged in their faces.” The turning is not an orderly retreat but the scattering of a terror-struck host.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, lifts the eye from the flight to the closing cry it prepares. After spreading its wings, they say, through twice three tetrastichs, the song now gathers itself and soars aloft in a final distich — a cry to God for victory on the king’s behalf, the arrows on the string and the enemies already turning. The witnesses do not divide over the picture: the foes who had plotted and could not perform are put to headlong flight, their backs to the king and their faces to the arrows, so that the very design they had bent against the throne recoils in their own rout.
13:
“Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength” — and the psalm that had traced every victory to God closes by asking him to display the power it has praised. The reformed John Gill reads the plea as a call for God to exert his strength and so be magnified for it, a lifting up he sees fulfilled by stages: at the destruction of Jerusalem, when the kingdom of God came with power; at the overthrow of Babylon, because strong is the Lord who judges her; and at the last day, when the wicked are punished with everlasting destruction from the glory of his power. The prayer for God’s exaltation is thus a prayer that runs out to the end of all things.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the paradox in the words and presses it: “Exalt thyself, O Lord — thy creatures cannot exalt thee. Lift thyself up, and discomfit thy foes by thine own strength.” God, he says, can give his people the victory over the most formidable enemies though they strike not a blow in their own defence, his right hand often winning the day while they stand still to see the salvation of God; and the closing “praise thy power” he turns into a rule of worship, that each believer celebrates most the attribute God has shown him most — wisdom to the taught, strength to the beset, mercy to the lost — so that the burden of every man’s song is the perfection by which he was himself delivered.

The grammatical-historical witnesses close the poem where it began, in address to God. Charles Ellicott notes that here “the song turns again to address Jehovah,” and renders the last line more fully, “we will both with song and lyre celebrate thy power.” Keil and Delitzsch hear the whole close soaring aloft and losing itself in this cry, “Be Thou exalted,” a plea that God would manifest that supernal and judicial sovereignty to which everything opposing him must yield, and for whose revealing the people promise beforehand a joyous gratitude. The witnesses do not divide: the psalm that opened with the king rejoicing in God’s strength ends with the whole company praying that same strength into full display and pledging, when it is shown, to answer it with song and lyre.
